text: Chapter 7, the unique ID generator. Let's see how it works in about three minutes.

When many machines hand out IDs at the same time, no two of them may ever issue the same number. Our requirements: IDs are unique, roughly sortable by time, fit in sixty-four bits, and we generate over ten thousand per second. Notice that unique, consecutive, and ordered are three different things. We don't need consecutive.

Option one: multi-master auto-increment. Two databases. One issues one, three, five. The other issues two, four, six. Both step by two, so there are no collisions. But database A may already be at one hundred and one while B is still at twenty, so the numbers don't match real time. And to add a third database, you can't just change the step.

Option two: UUID. Every server generates its own, with no coordination, so it scales easily. But a UUID is one hundred and twenty-eight bits. It doesn't fit in sixty-four, and a random UUID doesn't sort by time. Even UUID version seven, which is time-ordered, is still one hundred and twenty-eight bits.

Option three: a ticket server, like a single take-a-number machine. Everyone comes here to get a number. It's simple, and it gives you numeric IDs. But it's a single point of failure. If the machine goes down, nobody gets a number. Adding more servers brings back synchronization and conflicts.

Option four: Twitter's Snowflake. It splits sixty-four bits into fields. One sign bit, always zero. Forty-one bits of millisecond timestamp. Five bits for the datacenter. Five for the machine. And twelve for a sequence number. Time sits in the high bits, so a bigger number means a later time, and IDs sort naturally.

Here's how one ID is built. Time, datacenter, machine, and sequence each shift into their own position, then combine. If any one of them differs, the ID differs. But if two machines share the same datacenter number and machine number, they will issue identical IDs.

Now, within a single millisecond. Time stops at one millisecond, and three requests arrive. Their sequence numbers are zero, one, and two. In the next millisecond, the sequence resets to zero. Twelve bits go up to four thousand and ninety-five. When they run out, you can't wrap around to zero. You must wait for the next millisecond.

One more risk: clock rollback. The clock gets corrected and jumps back a few milliseconds. If you keep issuing IDs, you create duplicates. The right way is to compare against the last issue time every time. A small rollback, wait until it catches up. A large one, refuse and raise an alert. Never quietly reset the sequence and carry on.

Let's check capacity. One machine can issue at most four thousand and ninety-six IDs per millisecond. That's about four point one million per second in theory, far above the ten thousand we need. Forty-one bits of milliseconds last about sixty-nine point seven years. Sixty-four bits is a fixed budget, so machines, lifetime, and throughput trade off against each other.

Now compare all four. Multi-master is simple, but hard to scale and not time-ordered. UUID needs no coordination, but it's too long. A ticket server is easy to understand, but it's a single point of failure. Snowflake fits in sixty-four bits, is roughly ordered, and scales. The price is managing machine IDs and clocks.
Remember three words: time, machine, sequence. Time gives the order. Machine tells nodes apart. Sequence prevents duplicates within one millisecond.
